articles.title: Meet Lucas Rojas, the 16-year-old Miami student who turned one inclusive kickball game into a six-team league with 40+ players and 60+ teen volunteers, then won a $10,000 national young hero prize
articles.summary: A single kickball game gave 16-year-old Miami student Lucas Rojas an idea that grew far beyond one afternoon on the field.
articles.body: A single kickball game gave 16-year-old Miami student Lucas Rojas an idea that grew far beyond one afternoon on the field. What began as a chance to bring people with special needs and student volunteers together through sport eventually became LINKball: Kickball for All, a free league with six teams, more than 40 players and more than 60 student volunteers. Rojas, a student at Christopher Columbus High School, created the programme after seeing the impact of an inclusive charity kickball game. According to Christopher Columbus High School, which detailed his journey, the initiative has now earned him national recognition and a $10,000 Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes.How one kickball game sparked an ideaRojas first became involved in inclusive sports through CCHS LINK, a service programme at Christopher Columbus High School in Miami. While volunteering at an inclusive charity kickball game, he saw how a simple sporting activity could bring students together with people with special needs. The experience stayed with him. Rather than treating the event as a one-time opportunity, Rojas began thinking about how an inclusive sports programme could continue throughout the year.By the spring of his freshman year, that idea had become LINKball: Kickball for All. The programme was created to give people with special needs an opportunity to participate in organised sport while also allowing high school students to volunteer, form connections and become part of the activity. What started as a relatively small initiative gradually developed into a recurring league.From four teams to sixLINKball initially brought together four teams, 20 players with special needs and about 40 student volunteers. The programme has since grown to six teams, with more than 40 players and more than 60 student volunteers involved. The growth has transformed LINKball from a single inclusive sporting event into an organised league with fall and spring seasons.The programme is structured around participation and connection. Players with special needs are able to take part in a team sport, while student volunteers work alongside them during games and activities. This allows the volunteers to do more than simply assist; they become teammates and participants in the same experience. The programme has provided players with opportunities to build friendships, become part of a team and enjoy playing a sport in an inclusive setting. For the student volunteers, the experience offers another form of service. They get to interact directly with the players and develop relationships that continue over multiple seasons.The young founder behind LINKballRojas' involvement goes beyond creating the idea. He has taken an active leadership role in developing the programme and is also president of CCHS LINK. The initiative reflects his approach to community service: identify an opportunity for people to connect, then create something that can continue rather than ending after a single event.Kickball also helped make the concept accessible. Unlike sports that require extensive equipment or specialised facilities, kickball can be organised around basic sporting equipment and an open playing area. That makes it possible for a larger group of students and players to participate together. The emphasis is not solely on competition. LINKball is designed around inclusion, participation and relationships, giving players the chance to return season after season.A $10,000 Barron Prize recognitionRojas' work has now received recognition beyond his Miami school community. In September 2026, he was named one of the 2026 winners of the Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes, a national award for young people who have made a significant positive difference to their communities or the environment. The 2026 Barron Prize recognised 25 young leaders between the ages of 8 and 18. Fifteen of those winners received $10,000 awards to support their education or continue their service work.Rojas was among the 15 recipients receiving the $10,000 award. He was selected from more than 750 second-round applicants. The recognition places his work alongside projects led by other young people across the United States. The annual prize highlights teenagers and children who have taken action on issues affecting their communities and created initiatives of their own. For Rojas, the award recognises the development of LINKball from an initial idea into an established programme involving dozens of players and volunteers.Why inclusive sport mattersAt the centre of LINKball is a straightforward idea: sport can provide a shared space where people who might not otherwise meet can participate together. For players with special needs, having a regular team and season gives them an opportunity to return to the same community repeatedly. The programme also creates space for friendships and social interaction beyond the game itself.Student volunteers benefit from that interaction as well. Instead of observing from the sidelines, they participate directly, helping create an environment where the players are treated as teammates. The programme therefore works in both directions. Players receive an opportunity to participate in sport, while volunteers gain experience working with and alongside people with different abilities. That approach has helped LINKball expand while keeping its original purpose intact.What began with one gameThe story of LINKball began with a single inclusive kickball event. Rojas could have simply volunteered, completed the activity and moved on to another project. Instead, the experience prompted him to consider what could happen if inclusive sport became a regular opportunity. That question eventually became a six-team league involving more than 40 players and more than 60 student volunteers. His $10,000 Barron Prize now gives the initiative national recognition while Rojas continues his high school years and his work with CCHS LINK.For the players and volunteers who take part, however, the significance of LINKball remains rooted in something much simpler than an award: having a place to play, meet others, form teams and return to the field together. What started with one kickball game has grown into a programme that gives inclusive sport a regular place in the community.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: An English artist paid £2,090 for a painting listed only as ‘in the style of’ Helen McNicoll; experts later proved it was her long-lost Bean Harvest, valued at £300,000 and sold for £174,000
articles.summary: An English artist and part-time art dealer who bought a wrongly labelled oil painting for £2,090 at a regional UK auction made a life-changing discovery
articles.body: An English artist and part-time art dealer who bought a wrongly labelled oil painting for £2,090 at a regional UK auction made a life-changing discovery when experts confirmed that the painting was a long-lost Impressionist masterpiece. The artwork had originally been listed only as "in the style of" Canadian Impressionist Helen McNicoll and was later valued by specialists at £300,000. It was eventually sold at auction for £174,000 to Canadian collector Pierre Lassonde, bringing the painting back into public view after more than a century. David Taylor bought the painting at an auction where it was kept in a cheap plastic 1960s frame. It also had a brass-coloured plaque with the title Women of the Fields. The plaque misspelled the artist's name as "McNicol" and said the painting was made in 1958, more than 40 years after McNicoll died in 1915. Despite these mistakes, Taylor noticed the high quality of the brushwork. According to a report by Artnet, he thought the farming scene looked as if it had been painted by "someone who really knows what they're doing".Uncovering a hidden signatureAfter taking the painting home and removing the cheap plastic frame, Taylor found a signature in the bottom-left corner that appeared to match McNicoll's handwriting. However, art records did not list a work called Women of the Fields among her known paintings. Unsure about the painting's history, Taylor contacted the team behind the BBC television programme Fake or Fortune?, led by art dealer Philip Mould and broadcaster Fiona Bruce. The programme began a detailed scientific and historical investigation to find out whether the painting was genuine. Technical tests compared Taylor's painting with a known McNicoll work, The Apple Gatherer, painted around 1911. Experts found that the same pigments had been applied in the same ways to the figures' faces and the foliage in the background of both paintings. Laboratory tests also found Red Lake pigment made from natural organic materials. Under ultraviolet light, the pigment produced a pink glow in matching patterns on both paintings. This showed that the artist had used the same types of materials and pigments.Tracking a lost centuryHistorical research for the programme revealed that McNicoll had painted a work called The Bean Harvest. It had been shown five times in Canada between 1912 and 1913 before disappearing from public records. Provenance research carried out during the BBC investigation showed that the painting had later entered the private collection of the Pine-Coffin family in Britain. Norman Pine-Coffin, a British painter, had exhibited at London's Royal Academy around the same time as McNicoll. This suggested that the two artists may have known each other and helped explain how the painting moved from Canada to Britain. After the painting was authenticated, Mould estimated that The Bean Harvest could sell for £300,000 on the open market. During the Fake or Fortune? programme, Bruce praised the painting for its "light and movement" and called McNicoll "a pioneer".A return to Canadian soilThe authenticated painting was later offered at Sotheby's in London, where Canadian philanthropist and art collector Pierre Lassonde bought it for £174,000. Lassonde, who had previously called the painting "magnificent", loaned it to public institutions so that people could see it again for the first time in 110 years. According to a media release from the Art Gallery of Hamilton in Ontario, Canada, the painting was placed on central display as part of the exhibition Helen McNicoll: An Impressionist Journey. The exhibition was organized by the Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec and adapted by the Art Gallery of Hamilton. In a statement released by the Art Gallery of Hamilton, Shelley Falconer, the institution's President and Chief Executive Officer, spoke about the importance of bringing the painting back to Canada. "We are extremely honoured to feature The Bean Harvest as part of Helen McNicoll: An Impressionist Journey," Falconer said. "This exhibition is a truly inspiring tribute to one of Canada's most important Impressionist painters, and we invite everyone to experience her remarkable work in person."Pioneer of light and formHelen McNicoll was born in Toronto in 1879. She lost her hearing at the age of two after suffering from scarlet fever. In 1902, she moved to England to study at the Slade School of Fine Art in London and later built her career in Europe. She was elected to the Royal Society of British Artists in 1913 and the Royal Canadian Academy of Arts in 1914. She died in 1915 at the age of 35 from complications linked to diabetes. The discovery has also been highlighted by the British Art Fair in its market assessments as an important example of valuable artwork being found after passing through regional auction houses without being properly identified.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ethiopia's army says it has repelled TPLF attacks in first comment on fresh Tigray fighting
articles.summary: The military says its soldiers inflicted casualties as fears grow of a resumption of a full-blown civil war.
articles.body:
Ethiopia's army says it has repelled attacks from Tigrayan forces and their allies in parts of the north of the country, in its first statement since fighting broke out on Wednesday.

The army said hostilities began in an area of Amhara region close to the border with Tigray, adding that its soldiers had inflicted heavy casualties and seized weapons.

The developments come as tensions between the federal government and Tigrayan leaders have sharply escalated over the last few days, raising fears that a devastating civil war could resume.

On Wednesday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which dominates the region, seized control of three airports from federal police.

The TPLF has not commented on the army's claims and the BBC has not been able to independently verify the army's claims.

The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas.

There are unconfirmed reports that TPLF forces have launched attacks in the neighbouring regions of Afar and Amhara.

A humanitarian source in Afar told AFP news agency on Thursday that Tigrayan forces had launched heavy artillery attacks as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the border with Tigray.

"We are in the situation of full-blown war now," TPLF vice-president Amanuel Assefa is quoted by the news agency as saying.

The latest escalation follows months of rising tensions between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government and Tigray authorities, who fought a devastating war from 2020 to 2022.

That ended in an African Union-brokered peace deal but over recent months both sides have been accusing each other of violating the agreement.

It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.

On Sunday, the TPLF announced an alliance with six other armed groups to oust the government.

Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray.

Residents of Tigray's main city of Mekelle told the BBC that local forces had taken over control of the city's airport from the national police early on Wednesday.

This followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray in recent days.

A Mekelle resident told the BBC's Newsday programme on Thursday there had been no clashes in the city, unlike in the previous war, with most fighting happening elsewhere.

"Mekelle is calm, except the stress from the people," said the resident, only identified as Fitsum for his safety. He added that the biggest problem was economic, with people not having enough cash.

"People are in a mood where they are distressed because it's been so difficult, so tough. The last seven or eight months the government has been denying budgets to the civil servants and all the banks were running out of cash."

Fitsum said people had been relying on mobile banking but with the risk of communications being cut off, "people are going to be in grave danger because there is almost no cash".

With the outbreak of war, people were limiting their movements and the city was all quiet - "it's like a curfew has been placed," he told the BBC.

articles.title: Straitcraft: How geography gives Iran leverage and could do the same for India
articles.summary: It has been more than 200 days since the US-Iran war began, and yet the conflict remains without a conclusion.
articles.body: It has been more than 200 days since the US-Iran war began, and yet the conflict remains without a conclusion. One can expect a superpower like the United States, with the biggest economy and overwhelming military might, to swiftly win the war. In reality, it looks for a table to negotiate, where Iran appears to have an equal say.Influence over Hormuz has given Iran a form of leverage disproportionate to its conventional economic and military weight, highlighting how geography can be strategised to shape geopolitical outcomes in one's favour. The strategic significance of this leverage extends beyond the Gulf. From Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb to the Malacca Strait, influence over maritime chokepoints can allow states, and sometimes non-state actors, to influence trade, energy flows, and the calculations of much larger powers.For India, the crisis in the west could offer a lesson in how maritime geography can be leveraged in the east.Operation epic ‘weary’?In late February, the global energy supply chain was disrupted after the US and Israel launched coordinated strikes against Iran under "Operation Epic Fury". According to the Institute for the Study of War, the combined US-Israeli force carried out nearly 900 strikes on Iranian targets within the first 12 hours of the campaign, one of which killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. By March one, the coalition had struck over 2,000 targets across Iran, achieving air superiority and significantly dismantling the country's nuclear, military and government infrastructure.With its missile, drone, and regional proxy capabilities severely degraded, ISW and its partner, the Critical Threats Project, assessed that Iran used maritime disruption in the Strait of Hormuz as a means of forcing concessions from the US and exerting pressure on the global economy.The US Energy Information Administration (EIA) analysis based on Vortexa tanker-tracking data found that oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz fell sharply from an average of 21.6 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 4.9 million barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026.Crude oil and condensate flows declined from 15.9 million b/d to 3.7 million b/d, while petroleum product flows fell from 5.7 million b/d to 1.1 million b/d. Additionally, LNG flows also dropped from 10.5 billion cubic feet per day to 0.8 billion cubic feet per day over the same period.According to officials and analysts cited by Reuters, Tehran is not pursuing a decisive military victory but rather a strategy of calibrated attrition.The logic is that if Iran can show the world that prolonging the conflict carries a heavy toll for the global economy, it can force Washington to weigh whether its objectives are still worth those costs. Analysts say the underlying aim is to persuade the US and its allies that containing the crisis is more expensive than simply accommodating Iran's demands over the Strait of Hormuz. Higher global crude prices feed directly into petrol prices, inflation, transport costs, and the cost of doing business,Additionally, when economies that are heavily dependent on imported energy face higher costs and supply uncertainty, they can create pressure on Washington to bring the conflict to an end.India, for instance, imports nearly 90 per cent of its Oil. Before the conflict, around half of its crude oil imports, amounting to nearly 2.5 to 2.7 million barrels a day, passed through the strait, coming mostly from Iraq, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Kuwait, BBC reported.Washington was forced to temporarily ease its restrictions on Russian crude imports to India, granting an initial 30-day waiver in March. US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said the measure was intended “to enable oil to keep flowing into the global market”, preventing a bigger energy crisis.More imports from Russia further eased the country's dependence on the Gulf chokepoint, with Russian oil tankers reaching Indian ports through the Red Sea's Bab el-Mandeb Strait, providing an alternative supply route that bypassed Hormuz.Passage through the Mandeb Strait has become one of the alternatives to Hormuz, but it comes with its own chokepoints.Bab-el-MandebWith Hormuz disrupted, Saudi Arabia sought to make greater use of its Red Sea infrastructure. According to EIA, total oil flows through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait increased sharply from 5.4 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 8.1 million barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026. Crude oil and condensate flows nearly doubled, rising from 3.2 million b/d to 6.1 million b/d.However, the wider Iran conflict has also spilled over into Yemen, putting the fragile calm between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned Houthis under renewed strain. The 2022 truce had significantly reduced hostilities between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, but the regional war has reopened the strategic fault lines. The Houthis have since intensified their military campaign along Yemen's Red Sea coast, bringing them closer to one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints.The significance of the advance lies in their increasing proximity to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Houthis captured the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha on September 10 and subsequently advanced towards the Bab el-Mandeb area, including Perim Island.Since then, their gains have strengthened their ability to exert pressure on shipping through the southern entrance to the Red Sea.The Iran-backed group also declared that their maritime operations are targeted, saying international shipping would be spared while Saudi vessels remained subject to a naval blockade.The Houthis, a lightly resourced non-state group compared to the Saudi state and its conventional military, did not need to match that power to threaten it. Mere control of a 13-square-kilometre island at the strait's narrowest point was enough to put Riyadh's alternative route at risk.A lesson for India?While India has economically suffered from the crisis, it could also offer a lesson in how geography can be utilised for strategic leverage against China, a conventionally powerful neighbour.The Strait of Malacca is the world’s busiest maritime chokepoint, carrying more than 100,000 vessel transits a year and roughly a quarter to a third of global seaborne trade by value. China is by far the largest single beneficiary and risk-bearer. Most of its seaborne crude oil, a large share of its LNG and other energy imports, and about two‑thirds of its total maritime trade pass through the strait.It is the narrowest in the Phillips Channel near Singapore, roughly 2.7 km wide and nearly 25 metres deep.India does not control the waterway, but its proximity to the Strait through the Andaman and Nicobar Islands gives it a position from which it can potentially influence one of the world's busiest maritime routes. This has also prompted debate in strategic circles over whether India could use its naval position to impose a blockade on Chinese shipping through the Malacca Strait in the event of a conflict.According to Dr Ashok Sharma, Visiting Fellow at the University of New South Wales Canberra at the Australian Defence Force Academy, the Malacca Strait represents a significant source of strategic leverage for India in its maritime competition with China.Speaking to TOI, Sharma explains how India's geography can be strategically weaponised."In a conflict, India could use this geographical advantage, together with surveillance, submarines, maritime patrol aircraft and surface forces, to monitor and potentially disrupt Chinese shipping and energy flows," Sharma said.Given China's substantial dependence on maritime trade and energy supplies passing through the Strait, he argues this creates an important vulnerability that India can potentially exploit as part of a broader sea-denial strategy.However, blocking the Malacca Strait outright is not the same as having the capability to merely threaten or deny its use, as the Strait is an international waterway, and India cannot simply "close it at will"."But in a major conflict, the ability to monitor shipping, hold vessels at risk and make passage dangerous or prohibitively costly could give India considerable strategic leverage," Sharma added.In that sense, Sharma compares India's position to Iran's leverage around Hormuz, though the geography is different. Iran is a littoral state bordering Hormuz, whereas India's advantage around Malacca comes primarily from its proximity through the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, and its growing naval capabilities.Crucially, India's position away from the Strait also works to its advantage. Unlike Iran, whose coastline lies exposed along Hormuz, India is not littoral to Malacca, meaning China cannot blockade Indian ports the way the US did to Iran. New Delhi further benefits from a vast tri-directional coastline, an advantage Tehran does not possess.India doesn't need to physically seal the Malacca Strait to exert pressure on China, Sharma said."The credible possibility of disruption during a conflict could itself become a strategic instrument".Geography can sometimes compensate for a significant gap in conventional power, especially in a globalised world where nations are interdependent for resources. A state does not necessarily need the largest economy or the strongest military to exert influence over a much more powerful adversary. Possessing a strategically located piece of geography and the capability to exploit it can allow a relatively weaker power to impose costs, create uncertainty, and shape the wider geopolitical landscape.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mark Zuckerberg rejects calls for industrywide AI slowdown
articles.summary: In an interview with NBC News chief tech analyst Joanna Stern, the Meta founder and CEO said he doesn’t think AI companies need to work together on a slowdown.
articles.body: Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg pushed back on calls for AI companies to work together to slow the pace of their products’ development, following warnings from inside AI labs of the potential for human annihilation via rogue technology. In an interview with NBC News’ chief tech analyst Joanna Stern, Zuckerberg said that leading AI companies could slow down or pause development of their own products if they felt the technology was unsafe. His position cuts against recent calls for coordinated action from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. “I don’t think that we need some kind of industrywide coordination,” Zuckerberg said. “I think that each lab needs to take the time, and when it sees that there are issues, you just take the time that you need internally to basically make sure that you’re proceeding safely.” His comments came during a wide-ranging discussion with Stern about Meta’s approach to AI, wearable devices and privacy. Zuckerberg expanded on comments he posted on X last week, distancing himself from Amodei and Altman’s calls to “pace” or regulate the speed of AI development. Zuckerberg staked out a defiant position amid growing concern about risks from advanced AI systems. In early September, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon set off a wave of pitched concerns when he resigned over fears that AI systems could spiral out of human control in the next few years. Amodei released an essay calling for intercompany efforts to “pace the frontier” of AI development, which Altman soon endorsed alongside Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis and xAI’s Elon Musk. Zuckerberg said there was no need for such efforts, which critics have said are a Trojan horse that could allow AI companies to shut out competition and take control of efforts to regulate the industry. “I happen to think that there’s plenty of commercial incentive to get this right,” he said. Amodei and Altman briefed the United Nations Security Council on Wednesday, using the session to make their case for cooperation on slowing down the rate of AI progress in order to have more time to develop adequate safety and monitoring measures. Speaking to Stern in California, Zuckerberg emphasized that customers would naturally flock to the products that served their purposes best and said that an unsafe or unwieldy product would scare away potential users. “If you’re building a product, people aren’t going to want to use it if it doesn’t do what they want,” he said. The company’s Muse AI agent, an autonomous AI assistant, has soared in popularity in recent weeks. Released on Sept. 8, it can perform a raft of actions on behalf of users — from booking plane tickets and replying to emails to compiling research briefs and canceling unused magazine subscriptions. Muse is now the most popular free offering on the Apple App and Google Play stores. Several AI companies — including Amazon and Nvidia — have also released their own AI agents since the first widespread consumer-facing agent, OpenClaw, burst onto the AI scene in November. As an example of Muse’s capabilities, Zuckerberg said his own Muse agent helped give feedback on his mixed martial arts performance by connecting to cameras watching over his workout area. “You’re basically going to have an extremely capable assistant who can understand the things that you care about,” Zuckerberg said. Rather than worry about distant apocalyptic scenarios from rapidly improving AI systems, Zuckerberg said, AI companies should focus on making sure their systems understand users’ desires and intents and handle that information with discretion. “Nailing those things are going to be the most important next things to align with what people actually want in the world,” Zuckerberg said. Zuckerberg pointed out that the Muse system is actually several agents working together — another Meta AI agent, called Sentinel, oversees and polices the main Muse agent. If the Sentinel observes the Muse agent potentially exceeding its remit, the oversight agent can alert users and ask for human permission before carrying out any further actions. “The AI agent needs to be trained from the ground up to have a sense of what information is OK to share and what isn’t,” Zuckerberg said. Muse and other AI agents have stoked privacy concerns, given the amount of information and access that users can provide to them, including linking email accounts, bank cards and more so they can act without human intervention. Zuckerberg said users’ information was safe with Meta, pointing to the company’s track record on privacy and WhatsApp’s encrypted messaging as evidence that users could trust Muse with their data. “We’ve shown that we have the ability to build those kinds of world-class, leading security systems,” Zuckerberg said, mentioning that Meta worked with a field-leading cryptographer behind the popular anonymous Signal messaging app to develop its own secure technology. “I think that’s something that people can feel very good about.” Taking stock of the larger AI landscape, Zuckerberg distanced himself from warnings from Coxon and other researchers that AI could cause human extinction within a few years. Instead, he highlighted how personalized AI systems could revolutionize human life — echoing his August essay about the dawn of personalized superintelligence. “There’s a lot of rhetoric that is filled with doom,” Zuckerberg said. “I’m quite optimistic about the fact that this is going to be a very positive future for everyone.”

articles.title: Watch live: Netanyahu to address UN amid US-Israel war in Iran
articles.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is among the notable leaders set to address the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday, with the U.S.-Israel war in Iran and fighting in Gaza set to loom large over his remarks. Netanyahu will hit the stage a day after Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian pushed back against President Trump’s threats…
articles.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is among the notable leaders set to address the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday, with the U.S.-Israel war in Iran and fighting in Gaza set to loom large over his remarks.

Netanyahu will hit the stage a day after Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian pushed back against President Trump’s threats at the U.N. , declaring Iran would “never bow our head” and saying Tehran remains open to diplomacy.

Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas is also set to address the gathering by video Thursday after the U.S. denied him a visa to attend in person. Tens of thousands of Palestinians were killed in Gaza after Israel launched a military campaign in response to Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attack.

Netanyahu faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity tied to Gaza. He has denied the allegations.

Day three of the U.N. General Assembly is set to begin at 9 a.m. EDT.

articles.title: Rare September Nor’easter set to slam East Coast with heavy rain, damaging winds
articles.summary: Millions across the Northeast are bracing for an intense, multi-day Nor’easter this weekend that is forecast to bring heavy rain and strong wind gusts to the East Coast.
articles.body: Millions across the Northeast are bracing for an intense, multi-day Nor’easter this weekend that is forecast to bring heavy rain and strong wind gusts to the East Coast. Forecast models still disagree on the storm’s exact track, but one thing is clear: wherever it goes, it will hit the region hard. Forecasters have high confidence in a long-duration onshore wind event that could bring significant coastal flooding. Coastal flood warnings and high wind watches are already in place along much of the East Coast, with more alerts likely to be issued throughout the day Thursday. The highest rainfall totals — 2 to 3 inches or more — are most likely from Rhode Island to eastern Massachusetts. Powerful winds, including gusts up to 50-60 mph, risk toppling power lines and trees. Small shifts in the storm’s track will determine where outages and downed trees are most likely to occur. Coastal flooding is expected to run 1 to 3 feet above high tide, and a full moon Saturday night could intensify the tides and worsen the flooding. Waves along the coast are expected to reach 12 feet in Ocean City, New Jersey, and up to 22 feet in New England. Moderate to major flooding is likely from North Carolina to Nantucket, Massachusetts, with southeastern Virginia — particularly the Virginia Beach-to-Norfolk area — at highest risk for major coastal inundation of 1 to 3 feet. Meanwhile, a separate storm is already pummeling the Eastern Seaboard, generating high winds and rough surf. In Massachusetts, residents were seen this week hauling their boats out of the bay, worried about high tides and flooding from the Nor’easter. One person told NBC News he’d been “prepping all week for both wind and water.” One couple even changed their wedding plans because of the storm — they had been set to marry this weekend on a Massachusetts beach. And the Boston Red Sox moved Sunday’s game — the season finale — up to Friday to avoid any weather-related delays or cancellations. In New Jersey, crews cleared debris from storm drains and flood-prone areas as emergency management officials urged residents to prepare for the incoming storm. Monmouth County Sheriff Shaun Golden recommended charging devices and stocking up on batteries ahead of possible power outages. Elsewhere in the country, days of heavy rain in the Southwest have triggered major flooding, sending muddy waters sweeping through the streets of New Mexico. The El Paso, Texas, fire department said it has responded to more than 50 storm-related calls. Off the coast of Hawaii’s Big Island, Tropical Storm Nolo threatens heavy rain and flash flooding, with more than 30 inches of rain possible in some areas. Extreme rainfall remains the storm’s biggest risk. Nolo currently has sustained winds of 50 mph and is expected to strengthen into a hurricane by Thursday night — potentially reaching Category 3 strength. As of the latest update, the storm was about 285 miles south of South Point, Hawaii, moving north at 2 mph. Nolo is not expected to make direct landfall in Hawaii, but it could come close enough to bring tropical-storm-force winds to the Big Island and Maui as early as Thursday night, with hurricane-force winds possible by Friday night.

articles.title: Rubio warns of Iraq ‘Balkanisation’: Is that a real threat?
articles.summary: US secretary of state’s warning comes after he and Trump met the Iraqi PM on the sidelines of the UNGA.
articles.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has warned that Iraq risks “Balkanisation” unless its armed factions are brought under state control.

He made the remarks to reporters at the Palace Hotel in New York City on Wednesday, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, after meeting Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi Tuesday night.

Rubio said Washington had no doubt about al-Zaidi’s commitment to disarming Iraqi armed groups, but called it a massive and difficult challenge.

He said at least three armed groups had disarmed and joined the national government, while at least one had been far less cooperative.

Bringing all weapons under state control, he said, would mean Iraq no longer had “independent forces operating and balkanising the country”.

So what does Rubio really mean? And is the breakup of Iraq a real threat? Here’s what you need to know:

It means a country breaking up into smaller, rival units, usually along ethnic or religious lines.

The term comes from the fragmentation of the Balkans as the Ottoman Empire collapsed in the early 20th century.

In Iraq’s case, it has often been used to describe concerns that the country could split along ethnic and sectarian lines.

However, what Rubio was pointing to was “fractures within the Iraqi state system” caused by Iran-aligned armed groups, Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow for Middle East Security at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told Al Jazeera.

These groups act as rivals to one another, “but also by serving as arteries for pro-Iranian regime interests inside Iraq by wielding parallel economic channels, political influence, and oil smuggling networks”, she said.

Not imminently, although interpretations differ on how seriously to take Rubio’s warning.

“Balkanisation as Rubio framed it means more that Iraq risks failing to become a centralised, stable state that can wean off Iranian interference – not that it faces imminent territorial partition,” Ozcelik said.

She described the armed groups as a “festering, now structural” challenge, and said they have “operated inside federal Iraq with near impunity”.

Zeidon Alkinani, a Middle East political analyst and founding director of the Arab Perspectives Institute, was more sceptical.

He told Al Jazeera that Rubio’s remark could be read “either as a pressure tactic to push the Iraqi government forward on the disarmament process, or as a sign of the administration’s limited understanding of Iraq and the wider region”.

He said disarmament was “a major turning point” in Iraq’s post-2003 politics, but “far from the greatest challenge Iraq has faced”, pointing to the 2003 United States invasion, the sectarian strife of 2006–2007, the war against ISIL (ISIS) from 2014 to 2017 and the 2017 Kurdish independence referendum as far graver threats to the country’s unity.

What do we know about Trump and Rubio’s meetings with al-Zaidi?

Rubio told reporters he first met with the Iraqi prime minister, and then US President Donald Trump met with him on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday evening.

Al-Zaidi’s office said in a statement that they discussed political, economic and investment cooperation as well as regional security.

Why is the timing of the meeting important?

It was the second meeting between the two leaders since July, when al-Zaidi promised at the White House that armed factions would have no justification after September 30.

That deadline has since slipped; al-Zaidi told The New York Times that disarmament would now run until June 30, 2027.

Alkinani said that the government is in “a highly delicate position”, as many Iraqis strongly support disarmament, having long seen armed groups outside state institutions as a central pillar of corruption, and as a way to curb Iranian influence.

That could give Baghdad “some breathing room” from both Washington and Tehran, he said, but “it remains an extremely difficult transformation that demands patience and political sensitivity; without them, the process could quickly unravel”.

The meeting also came days before the remaining few hundred US troops are due to leave Iraq on September 30.

Rubio told reporters on Wednesday that “there’s been no discussion” on extending that timeline.

Most of Iraq’s armed groups come under the umbrella of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), a mostly Shia body formed to fight ISIL (ISIS).

The PMF was formally brought into Iraq’s security forces a decade ago, but many of its factions keep their own command structures and maintain close ties to Iran.

Several groups say they have complied with the government’s push.

Saraya al-Salam, Asaib Ahl al-Haq and Kataib al-Imam Ali have reached understandings with Baghdad to hand over their weapons or regularise their status.

Saraya al-Salam, the armed wing linked to Shia leader Muqtada al-Sadr, was formally integrated into the security forces at a ceremony in Samarra in June.

But Ozcelik cautioned that “full disarmament of any group has not really been fully, successfully implemented yet”.

The most powerful Iran-aligned factions have refused. Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba say they will keep what they call “resistance weapons”.

Hadi al-Amiri, the leader of the Badr Organisation, one of the oldest and largest factions, said last month that bringing weapons under state control was an Iraqi decision, not one imposed from outside, and ruled out any clash between the state and “the resistance”.

Ozcelik said the challenge now is “discerning which of these groups – they have their own sets of interests, pockets, and incentives – can credibly be incorporated and which cannot by the disarmament deadline”.

A key test, she added, will be whether al-Zaidi can “Iraq-ify these groups, meaning a transition to an Iraq-first or Iraqi-Shia identity”.

Have the armed groups played a role in the Iran war?

Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba have both previously targeted US forces in Iraq and have attacked Gulf states during the US-Israel war on Iran.

On Wednesday, Rubio said recent strikes on energy infrastructure in the region were probably carried out in part by Iran-backed armed groups in Iraq, not only by Yemen’s Houthis.

“Pro-Iran militias have directly played a destabilising role in the US-Iran confrontation,” said Ozcelik, citing reports that Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline was targeted from southern Iraq.

Are Iranian airlines still flying to Iraq?

New US sanctions threaten to cut off any airport or company that refuels, services or sells tickets for Iranian airlines.

Iran says Baghdad has stopped accepting its flights and is trying to reroute them to Najaf, where flights to Iran are continuing, and no suspension order has been received.

Najaf, home to the shrine of Imam Ali, is a major destination for pilgrims, and local travel companies depend heavily on routes to Iran.

articles.title: Did AI-enabled ‘kill chain’, outdated intel lead to deadly Iran school strike? What report claims
articles.summary: Outdated intelligence, a rushed targeting process and reliance on an AI-enabled system may have contributed to the deaths of more than 150 people,
articles.body: Outdated intelligence, a rushed targeting process and reliance on an AI-enabled system may have contributed to the deaths of more than 150 people, including at least 123 children, in a US missile strike on a school in Iran’s Minab in February.The findings do not establish that artificial intelligence independently selected the school as a target. Instead, investigators have identified a series of failures across the US military's targeting process, including outdated satellite imagery, intelligence that was not properly updated, reduced civilian-harm checks and reliance on the AI-enabled Maven Smart System to help process information and prioritise targets, according to a Bloomberg report.The Pentagon has not publicly accepted responsibility for the strike and has said the incident remains under investigation. The full findings of the probe, which began in March, have not been released.Maven, developed by Palantir Technologies, has become a central part of US military operations, combining information from more than 150 data sources to help personnel assess potential targets and coordinate operations. Officials involved in the investigation said some personnel appeared to expect the system to identify inconsistencies or stale information in the intelligence supplied to it.AI-enabled kill chainThe Minab site had reportdly been classified in the US military's main intelligence database as an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps facility. But the site had changed significantly over the years and had been operating as a school.Commercial satellite imagery showed that walls and entrances had been built to separate the school from the military compound, with a soccer pitch and other visible signs of civilian use. One US intelligence analyst had identified changes at the site as early as 2019, but those observations were recorded in a system that was not connected to the primary database used for targeting.The investigation also found that the US military was working under intense time pressure before the February 28 assault. More than 1,000 Iranian targets were struck during the first 24 hours, and work that would normally take much longer to assess and approve potential targets was compressed into days or even minutes, according to officials familiar with the probe.The Minab site emerged as one of the recommended targets.The military's targeting process, known as the "kill chain", involves multiple stages. Intelligence analysts assess potential targets, imagery specialists examine the site, weapons planners determine how to conduct the strike, lawyers assess whether the target qualifies as a lawful military objective and commanders ultimately approve the attack.Maven is now a crucial part of that process, helping bring together intelligence and other information for military personnel.Officials involved in the investigation said the Minab site passed through the various stages with high confidence that it was an IRGC facility. "Minab proved you should never be too confident," one Pentagon official involved in the probe said, as quoted by Bloomberg.Investigators have also examined the reduction in Pentagon teams responsible for assessing civilian harm. Officials said staffing across those units had been cut sharply, with the Central Command team reduced from 10 members to one.No member of the team reviewed the Minab site before the strike, according to officials familiar with the investigation. Such reviews had previously been used to assess civilian activity around potential targets and identify ways to reduce the risk to noncombatants.Pentagon changes processThe role of Maven has come under particular scrutiny because of its growing importance to US military targeting. Palantir, however, has rejected responsibility for the intelligence that was fed into the system.The company said it "is not responsible for the underlying data nor identifying intelligence deficiencies" and that there was no evidence its software was at fault in the Minab strike.Since the attack, US Central Command has changed parts of its targeting process. The changes include additional procedures to refresh and vet planned targets, new open-source data feeds to provide more information about civilian activity and dozens of upgrades to Maven.Palantir has also added capabilities that allow the system to re-examine underlying intelligence and flag inconsistencies or inaccuracies that may have been missed during human review, according to people familiar with the changes.Cameron Stanley, head of the Pentagon's digital and artificial intelligence office, said the upgrades reflected lessons from the conflict."Different types of things were identified, different challenges were identified, new data sources were incorporated," Stanley said.The investigation comes as the United Nations has separately raised concerns about the strike. A UN fact-finding mission said this week that there were reasonable grounds to conclude that the Minab attack and another US strike amounted to war crimes; a finding US has declined to acknowledge.You use AI every day. articles.title: First baby born on remote Scottish island in more than 30 years
articles.summary: A baby has been born on the remote Scottish island of North Ronaldsay for the first time in more than three decades.
articles.body: A baby has been born on the remote Scottish island of North Ronaldsay for the first time in more than three decades. Duncan Wilder Thorstein Traill Suarez Ford was born on September 15, marking the first birth on the island in 34 years, his mother Alice Traill Ford told CNN on Thursday. North Ronaldsay is Orkney’s most northerly island, and is only three miles long and two miles wide. Traill Ford, fiancé Jorge Suarez and family split their time between Costa Rica and North Ronaldsay, and the original plan was for Duncan to be born in Costa Rica, she said. The family had return flights booked when they arrived in North Ronaldsay, but the birth plan changed when they landed. “I knew instantly that it would be the most special, magical and supportive birth that I could give him,” said Traill Ford, whose family bought the island 1727. “My connection to the island is what brings me back every year,” she said. “Every year since I was a baby.” “I feel this island had a hand in raising me and it’s for that reason that I felt the greatest sense of connection and belonging with the energy here, especially in my ancestral home,” added Traill Ford, who gave birth at Holland House, which was built by her ancestors. According to Scottish government figures in 2024, the island’s population was 72. Traill Ford told CNN there are now 51 people living on North Ronaldsay. “Everybody’s very excited,” said Traill Ford, who gave out small bottles of whisky decorated with four leaf clovers and small shells known locally as groatie buckies, which are meant to bring good luck. “They’re kind of extended family, it feels like… a giant family, island family, distant relatives,” she added. As for why no children have been born on the island in so long, Traill Ford believes that it may be due to a lack of healthcare facilities, with no doctor or hospital, and only a resident nurse “I believe it’s because people feel maybe afraid of the things that might be able to go wrong in childbirth and so they feel safer being in a hospital where everything is available for the support that they may need in case something were to go wrong,” she said, adding that it takes around two hours and 40 minutes to reach the mainland of Orkney by boat. “If you’re in an emergency then the coast guard helicopter would fly out for you otherwise if you’re well enough then you would need to travel into Kirkwall (on) the mainland,” she said.

Duncan is the first baby born on the island in 34 years.

articles.title: Florida deputies taser sword-wielding burglary suspect, video shows
articles.summary: Bodycam video captured the tense moment deputies in Florida tasered sword-wielding suspect Josiah Smith after he allegedly refused commands.
articles.body: Police in Florida released tense body camera video showing the moment a sword-wielding burglary suspect was tased by deputies after allegedly refusing to drop the weapon. The Alachua County Sheriff's Office said they responded early Tuesday in Gainesville after a "caller stated a man forced his way into their home with a sword, and they were forced outside against their will by the intruder." "Hey, brother, do me a favor, drop the sword. Drop the sword on the ground, my man. Let me talk to you, OK? articles.title: Dee Brock, original director of the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders, dies at age 96
articles.summary: Dee Brock, the original director of the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders who helped mold the prototype for NFL sideline entertainment, died on Wednesday, the team said.
articles.body: Dee Brock, the original director of the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders who helped mold the prototype for NFL sideline entertainment, died on Wednesday, the team said. She was 96. Former Cowboys cheerleader Kelli Finglass – now the team’s director – called Brock a “visionary who helped create an icon.” “Dee’s leadership, imagination and unwavering commitment to excellence shaped far more than a team. She created a standard, a spirit and a symbol that have inspired generations and earned recognition around the world,” Finglass said in a statement. “Her influence lives on in every performance, every dream pursued and every woman who has ever worn the uniform with pride. We are deeply grateful for her vision, her courage and the extraordinary legacy she leaves with the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders.” Finglass added: “Rest peacefully, Dee. You will always be remembered and your legacy will continue to shine.” When the squad was first formed in 1961, Brock according to the team’s history, “utilized high school students with traditional cheers to lead the crowd.” The team added “dance elements” to its game-day routine in 1965, then in 1972 introduced its now-iconic uniforms — boots, short shorts and a fringed, midriff bearing top — which has remained virtually unchanged since. Brock retired in 1975. The team honored Brock in 2022 with a lifetime achievement award, presented as a rhinestone-adorned football. “I hadn’t realized I had made such a good impression, and I’m so happy about that,” Brock told NBC affiliate KETK during the presentation ceremony at her Tyler home. Brock’s advocacy is credited with helping integrate the cheerleading squad. “The kindness that she showed, the encouragement, the warmth to a 16-year-old high school girl, it’s amazing what encouraging words, what kindness can do.” said Eunice Cicero, a pioneering member of the 1965 squad. “Thanks to Dee, I had the pleasure of being one of the first African American cheerleaders for the Dallas Cowboys.”

articles.title: Min Zin’s freedom must be first on the Trump-Xi summit agenda
articles.summary: Former Senate staffer Ellen Bork urged President Trump to demand the release of wrongfully detained Americans Min Zin and Youlin Chen during his summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
articles.body:
As the summit meeting between President Trump and China’s General Secretary Xi Jinping gets under way today, the first item on the agenda must be freedom for Min Zin, an American expert on Myanmar, who has been detained in China since June 3.

Min Zin, 53, was already in China, if only barely, when he was arrested at the Kunming airport upon his arrival to participate an academic workshop. The Chinese government announced it was investigating him for “endangering national security.”

The charge is absurd and raises questions about why Beijing moved against him after he had previously visited China without incident.

Certainly, Zin has the kind of background autocratic regimes dislike. As a teenager, he participated in Burma’s pro-democracy protests of 1988. Although violently crushed by the military, the protests brought Burma’s democracy movement to international prominence and to the forefront of American policy toward the country. (Myanmar is the official name for the country although Burma, the anglicized version, remains widely used.)

Zin’s career has been in research and academia. After arriving in the U.S. he married, became a U.S. citizen and pursued a Ph.D. at the University of California-Berkeley.

Like many other exiles, Zin returned to Burma when limits on the media, political activity and education were eased in 2011. He founded the Institute for Strategy and Policy-Myanmar , one of the country’s first independent think tanks in 2016. However, when a military coup overthrew the elected government in 2021, Zin and the institute relocated to Thailand.

In January, I met Zin at his office in northern Thailand. I found him thoughtful, intellectual and entirely focused on policy solutions to Burma’s many problems. That requires attention to Beijing’s growing influence in Burma which it borders. His institute has documented the role Chinese transnational criminal organizations and state-affiliated actors play in Burma’s multibillion-dollar scam centers and China’s appetite for its rare earth minerals.

Since the military unseated the elected government, Myanmar has seen an unprecedented level of armed conflict pitting multiple ethnic and pro-democracy forces against the regime. The conflict threatens China’s interests there, especially the deep-water port it is building at Kyaukphyu on Burma’s southwest coast. Kyaukphyu gives Beijing access to the Indian Ocean and could reduce China’s dependence on the Strait of Malacca upon which Beijing currently relies for 80 percent of its oil .

Recent gains by Burmese rebels in the area around Kyaukphyu may have led Beijing to seek to ingratiate itself with Myanmar’s government. Daniel Swift, a former U.S. diplomat in Myanmar, speculates that Beijing arrested Zin as an “ offering ” to Burma’s junta — “a public demonstration of loyalty” just before the visit to China of Min Aung Hlaing, the former general running Burma’s military-backed government later that month. In fact, Beijing announced Min Zin’s arrest and Min Aung Hlaing’s visit on the same day.

But if arresting an American citizen helps Beijing manage its relations with Myanmar, it should immeasurably complicate relations with the Trump administration. American academics and tourists alike must now reconsider their plans to visit China. They must also be aware that Beijing reaches across borders to harass and forcibly repatriate its critics in other countries where it cultivates influence.

China’s political system and repression consistently earn a “not free” rating from Freedom House , which cites the Chinese Communist Party’s domination of the judicial system and the absence of due process in criminal proceedings. Zin’s wife, Sylvia Zin, gave a harrowing account of her husband’s detention to a subcommittee of the House Foreign Affairs Committee on Sept. 16. He has undergone lengthy interrogations, confinement in a small cell lit 24 hours a day and interruption of his Buddhist meditation. He has not been allowed access to a lawyer.

The U.S. State Department has designated both Min Zin and Youlin Chen , an American seismologist held by China since 2024, “wrongfully detained” a status which raises the priority on their cases and commits resources to help them and their families. China mocked that finding with its foreign ministry spokesman claiming, “China is a country governed by the rule of law, and there is no such thing as so-called wrongful detention.”

Only consequences for detaining American citizens will lead China to free Min Zin and Chen. Trump should inform Xi of these when they sit down to talk and insist that the men be sent on their way home before Xi’s plane takes off from the U.S.

Ellen Bork is a former senior staff member for Asia on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. She has written extensively about American policy in support of democracy and human rights in China.

articles.title: Congressman says Venezuelan man shot by ICE then taken into custody told he needs surgery
articles.summary: U.S. Rep. Greg Casar said Wilber Rafael Garces Perez was in a wheelchair and still in pain, but did not say whether the family had decided that he should undergo surgery.
articles.body: AUSTIN, Texas — A Democratic congressman said Wednesday that a Venezuelan man shot by a federal immigration officer in Texas and then taken to a detention center has been told by a specialist he needs surgery to remove the bullet still lodged near his spine. U.S. Rep. Greg Casar visited a federal detention center in south Texas where Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, was taken into custody after being shot Sunday in Austin by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent. Casar said Garces Perez was in a wheelchair and still in pain, but did not say whether the family had decided that he should undergo surgery. The Department of Homeland Security has said Garces Perez, who has been taken to a hospital twice since the shooting, is receiving around-the-clock medical care and pain medication. “If they want to say it’s great medical care, they should start providing great medical care today by having him leave the detention center, go to a hospital or to a doctor, and do not delay his surgery if that’s what his family chooses to do,” Casar said. Garces Perez remains in Texas detention center Casar, whose district includes Austin, was the first member of Congress to visit Garces Perez in person since the shooting. He said the wound in Garces Perez’s back remains bloody and medical staff change his gauze two or three times daily. Following Casar’s visit and a press conference, DHS issued a previous statement denying claims that Garces Perez was forced to sleep on a floor or that he was prevented from having the bullet removed, saying ICE would not advise on a medical procedure for a detainee. Garces Perez was making a DoorDash delivery when ICE officers in an unmarked truck sideswiped his car twice, his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said. He was shot and taken to a hospital, then released into ICE custody with a bullet still in his back, she said. ICE and DHS haven’t said what led to the shooting beyond that Garces Perez was “the subject of a targeted vehicle stop.” ICE has not said if the agent who fired was wearing a body camera. At the beginning of September, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he expected all field agents to have them by the end of the month. Austin police released body camera footage from its officers who arrived just after the shooting. Garces Perez is seen hunched over in the front seat of his car and grabbing his shoulder and rocking back and forth. An officer later cut off Garces Perez’s shirt, and a wound can be seen in his upper back. Garces Perez entered the U.S. in 2024 using CBP One, a program begun under President Joe Biden that allowed migrants to make appointments with U.S. authorities to be considered for asylum, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. President Donald Trump ended the program on his first day in office. Garces Perez was an asylum seeker and had a valid work permit, according to Lincoln-Goldfinch. She said a judge issued a deportation order after Garces Perez missed an immigration court hearing because the notice was sent to a former address. ICE crackdown in Austin sees more than 1,000 arrests Garces Perez’s shooting came at the end of a summer in which ICE notably ramped up enforcement operations in Austin and surrounding suburbs and increasingly targeted immigrants without criminal records in public places. In all, ICE made more than 1,000 arrests in Austin, Pflugerville and other nearby cities during June and July, more than an 80% increase from a year earlier, which had been the previous peak, according to ICE data provided to the Deportation Data Project at the University of California, Berkeley, and the University of California, Los Angeles, and analyzed by The Associated Press. Unlike some other places, the increases in Austin were not driven by partnerships with local law enforcement agencies or by picking up jail inmates. Instead, the data shows that ICE officers made the vast majority of arrests in the community through traffic stops and other enforcement methods. Nearly 2 out of 3 people who were arrested in the Austin area had no criminal convictions and no pending criminal charges, the data shows.

articles.title: Bolton: ‘Trump just wants to announce deals’ during Xi visit
articles.summary: John Bolton, President Trump’s former national security adviser, said Wednesday Trump “just wants to announce deals” during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the White House. In an interview on NewsNation, host Leland Vittert asked Bolton if Americans should believe the outcomes or announcements from meetings between Chinese and U.S. leaders. “Not really until you…
articles.body:
John Bolton, President Trump’s former national security adviser, said Wednesday Trump “just wants to announce deals” during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the White House.

In an interview on NewsNation, host Leland Vittert asked Bolton if Americans should believe the outcomes or announcements from meetings between Chinese and U.S. leaders.

“Not really until you see it become operational,” Bolton said. “There are serious issues here that I can guarantee Xi Jinping has come fully prepared on each and every one of them. He knows what he thinks China’s interests are. Trump just wants to announce deals.”

“Whether the deals happen or not is really secondary. Many of them couldn’t happen just because of their complexity until after he leaves office. And if they don’t happen, he’ll just blame it on somebody else,” he continued.

Bolton added that “meetings per se don’t do anything” and that it should be more of “a question of what they produce.”

During Xi’s visit to the nation’s capital , he and U.S. officials are expected to discuss trade and the rapidly evolving artificial intelligence industry .

The visit comes less than two months before a Nov. 10 deadline to extend the current trade truce from last year, which Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday would now extend until January.

It is also the Chinese leader’s first state visit to the U.S. in more than a decade.

Bolton said the focus “dealing with the Chinese on AI is a fool’s air” as “they’re not worried about the doomsday scenarios that I think are motivating a lot of the calls in the U.S. for regulation of AI.”

“I think we’re missing what the Chinese agenda is,” Bolton added.

Trump stated on social media Thursday that artificial intelligence “will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China’s position also. Our guardrail is the DOJ [Department of Justice]!”

He contrasts warnings from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei who urged global cooperation on AI safeguards during their speeches at the United Nations Security Council.

articles.title: Cheshire's Tatton Park Apple Day cancelled after poor harvest
articles.summary: It is the first time the event has been cancelled in 24 years.
articles.body:
Tatton Park's annual Apple Day has been cancelled for the first time in 24 years after extreme weather and increased pest activity left organisers short of fruit to share with visitors.

The event in Cheshire will not take place this October following a significantly reduced harvest from the estate's collection of about 300 apple and pear trees.

Head gardener Simon Tetlow said prolonged summer drought had created one of the most challenging growing seasons the team had experienced.

He said the cancellation highlighted the challenges climate change posed for sustainable fruit growing.

Head gardener Simon Tetlow said: "For 24 years, our orchards have provided the centrepiece for a fantastic tasting day to celebrate the start of autumn, but this year a combination of prolonged drought and unprecedented pest pressures has left us without enough fruit to share with visitors."

He said the gardening team was already adapting what crops were grown, where they were planted and cultivation methods to improve resilience in future seasons.

Organisers said they hoped Apple Day would return in 2027.

articles.title: Inter-island matches costing sports clubs up to £10k
articles.summary: Channel Island fixtures under threat due to the cost and infrequency of travel between the islands.
articles.body:
Sport representatives in the Channel Islands say inter-island fixtures are under threat due to the cost and infrequency of travel between the islands.

A proposed summer ferry service between Jersey and Guernsey was withdrawn by the operator after being rejected by Guernsey's Committee for Economic Development.

Jersey's football team has been quoted a cost of £10,000 to play the Muratti semi-final in Alderney next March.

Guernsey Football Association chief executive Gary Roberts said: "For all these grassroots clubs and sports, those are significant costs, so anything the governments can do to help with timetables and costs and support for sport would be greatly appreciated."

The lack of frequent scheduled services between the most southerly and northerly of the islands means Jersey must go to Alderney via Guernsey, adding cost and time.

"Because of the way that the flights don't connect with each other, we'd actually have to be away for two nights for one 90-minute game of football," Jersey Football Association chief executive Tim Pryor said.

"So that's just one example of the sort of costs we're talking about."

Jersey and Guernsey football sides face one another in two inter-island cups - the Jersey-organised Wheway Cup and Guernsey's Jeremie Cup - which Roberts said would cost "upwards of £3,000 for a single match".

Jersey's football team has had to pull out of its annual Under 21 game against Guernsey following the end of a sponsorship arrangement.

Jersey's former England netball captain Serena Kersten was elected to the island's government earlier this year.

She has responsibility for sport in her brief as assistant minister in the Infrastructure, Education and Economic Development department.

"I felt the pains of this as well from a Jersey netball perspective so I share the frustration," she said

DFDS took over Jersey's ferry service last year but does not provide a route to Guernsey.

Asked if she would like to see an inter-island link between the islands from DFDS, she said: "I think we all would love that but there are obviously consequences and unintended consequences to all of these decisions.

"I know it's not been looked into this quarter, but I think it is something that we all know it needs to be looked into, but timing is important and making sure that we're having the right conversations first before we make any decisions is really, really important."

Economic Development minister deputy Gerald Voisin said in a written question there are no planned revisions to the concession agreement but it is kept under review regularly .

Kersten said she was hoping for positive solutions: "We can't go on with this for four years and I'm very well aware of that."

DFDS, Aurigny and Islands Unlimited have been contacted for a comment.

Brittany Ferries, which runs Guernsey's ferries, said it has complied with the terms of its contract signed last April and recognised the important of inter-island connectivity for sport.

Guernsey's Committee for Economic Development confirmed it met its Jersey counterparts earlier this week and the groups expressed their continued commitment to inter-island connectivity.

articles.title: More Americans hold positive views of China: Survey
articles.summary: A new survey found more Americans hold a positive view on China than in 2021, as Chinese President Xi Jinping visits the U.S. for the first time in more than a decade. The Pew Research survey asked people to rate China, along with other countries, on a “feeling thermometer” ranging from 0 to 100, where…
articles.body:
A new survey found more Americans hold a positive view on China than in 2021, as Chinese President Xi Jinping visits the U.S. for the first time in more than a decade.

The Pew Research survey asked people to rate China, along with other countries, on a “feeling thermometer” ranging from 0 to 100, where a low score correlates to a “cold and negative” feeling.

Americans give China an average rating of 37, up from 28 in 2021, when the country was coming out of the coronavirus pandemic that many blamed on Beijing. The share of respondents with a warm view of China, which is defined as a score of 51 and above, increased from 11 percent in 2021 to 19 percent this year.

Neutral views, or those rated at exactly 50, increased from 20 percent to 27 percent. The share of respondents with cold views, at 49 and below, fell from 68 percent to 54 percent. Those with very cold views, at 24 and below, also dropped from 47 percent to 34 percent.

The survey results noted that Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents have significantly warmer views of China than Republicans and Republican-leaning independents do at 43 percent and 29 percent, respectively.

Still, people in both parties have warmer views toward China in the new survey than in the last one. For Democrats, 26 percent held a warm view compared with 15 percent in 2021, while 10 percent of Republicans held a warm view, doubling the 5 percent seen in 2021.

The results come as bilateral talks begin between U.S. and Chinese leaders, which are expected to concern the development of artificial intelligence and trade issues. In his Thursday remarks, Xi said that both countries share a responsibility “to develop and manage AI for good and ensure that a development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people.”

President Trump stated before Xi arrived that he wanted to leave AI “exactly where it is. That is China’s position also.”

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced Wednesday that U.S. and Chinese officials agreed to extend their trade truce by two months. The truce extends lower U.S. tariffs on Chinese exports, and China agreed to suspend its export controls on rare earth metals.

The Pew Research survey of 5,193 U.S. adults was conducted Sept. 14-20. The margin of error was 1.6 percentage points.

articles.title: Xi says China, US have ‘responsibility’ to keep AI under human control
articles.summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping said Thursday the U.S. and China have an obligation to manage the development of artificial intelligence as “leading nations” in the industry. “We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the…
articles.body:
Chinese President Xi Jinping said Thursday the U.S. and China have an obligation to manage the development of artificial intelligence as “leading nations” in the industry.

“We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people,” Xi said in the White House’s Grand Foyer.

For his part, Trump said he and Xi will discuss AI, which Trump has taken to calling “ super intelligence .”

“The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come,” he said.

Earlier Thursday, Trump wrote on Truth Social that it would be a “big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is.”

“That is China’s position also. Our guardrail is the DOJ,” Trump wrote, referring to the Department of Justice.

The president has repeatedly said the only guardrail needed is the department, despite many industry officials calling for new safeguards.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei both appeared before the United Nations Security Council on Wednesday and urged global cooperation on AI safeguards.

“In our history, there have been times where countries who compete and don’t always like each other very much still come together for shared interests and the collective good in the face of a powerful new technology,” Altman said. “We believe this must be one of those times.”

But Trump suggested in his speech that the U.S. “totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme” on AI.

Trump has also maintained the U.S. needs to win the race on AI development. He has called any concerns of the technology hurting humanity a “hoax.”
